newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy sounds death knell for once mighty IRI.
newsitem.headline: Italy sounds death knell for once mighty IRI.

text.p: The days of Italy's once mighty state industrial conglomerate IRI look numbered after the government signalled it would strip the group of its highly profitable telecom interests -- Stet and Telecom Italia.
"They have pulled the plug on IRI. This is the beginning of the process," Giovanna Mossetti, an economist with Milan brokerage Caboto, said on Tuesday.

Newspapers on Tuesday hailed a Treasury decision to merge Stet, a holding company for telecom interests, with its main operating arm Telecom Italia, and to remove them from the IRI stable as the twilight of state involvement in industry.
"Farewell IRI, SuperStet is born," headlined Rome daily La Repubblica. "The defeat of IRI encircled by debts," read a headline in Milan business daily Il Sole 24 Ore.
The Treasury move is a prelude to the privatisation of an enlarged Stet which, pending completion of the merger by May 1997, is unlikely to go ahead until the autumn of next year.
The government had hoped to sell off Stet by the spring but legislation to enact a regulatory authority to police the telecommunications industry is still languishing in parliament.

A statement issued by the Treasury on Monday after Treasury minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi met EU Commissioner Karel Van Miert in Brussels to discuss plans for privatising Italian state companies effectively sounded the death knell for IRI.
The Italian government "considers that IRI's mission as a public holding of big industrial and service companies operating under state monopoly has come to an end," the statement said.

The shock decision by the Treasury to seize IRI's crown jewels came as pressure mounted from Brussels on the Italian government to restore order to IRI's accounts which are sagging under a mountain of debt.

Under a 1993 accord with the European Union, the government was committed to slashing IRI's debt to below five trillion lire ($3.3 billion) by the end of the year. At the end of 1995 IRI's debt totalled 22.5 trillion lire.
The Treasury is expected to take some 11-12 trillion lire of debts off IRI's balance sheet, in return for IRI's 64 percent stake in Stet's ordinary share capital.

IRI's stake in Stet, which holds a dominant shareholding both in Telecom Italia and cellular phone operator Twelecom Italia Mobile, has a book value of some 11.2 trillion lire, Italian newspapers reported.
The state conglomerate has also been ordered by the Treasury to privatise profitable toll-road operator Autostrade and to sell off minority stakes in shipping company Finmare and Banca di Roma.

IRI will be left with a rump made up of companies which will also have to be disposed off in due course -- loss-making state airline Alitalia, shipbuilder Fincantieri, engineering and defence group Finmeccanica and state broadcaster RAI.

For IRI, set up in the 1930s by fascist dictator Benito Mussolini, it is a sad end for what was the biggest industrial enterprise in the western world employing 600,000 people in its heyday in the 1960s.
The company played a crucial role in Italy's postwar reconstruction, building motorways, cars, ships, railways and wiring up the country with a modern telecommunications network.
But it went into decline in the 1970s as politicians milked the group as a source of patronage and ailing companies were systematically parked on IRI's books to save them from bankruptcy.
